sections.title: What is a WHO guideline?

summary.text: Defines a WHO guideline as any WHO document containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy. Explains that a recommendation tells the intended user what to do in specific situations to achieve the best health outcomes and helps users decide, select and prioritize among interventions.

sections.extract: A WHO guideline is any document developed by the World Health Organization containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy. A recommendation tells the intended end-user of the guideline what he or she can or should do in specific situations to achieve the best health outcomes possible, individually or collectively. sections.title: Why does WHO develop guidelines?

summary.text: Explains that WHO develops guidelines when Member States, country offices, experts or other stakeholders ask for guidance because they are unsure what to do. Lists the triggers of such uncertainty: a new problem or emergency, new evidence, a lack of good evidence, or a change in resources or access to services.

sections.extract: WHO develops guidelines whenever Member States, WHO country offices, external experts or other stakeholders ask for guidance on a clinical or public health problem or policy area. This generally happens when they are uncertain about what to do or how to choose among a range of potential policies or interventions. sections.title: What principles underlie WHO guidelines?

summary.text: Describes the principle that WHO is a science- and evidence-based organization, citing its general programme of work. States that guidelines are the main means of exercising technical leadership and that WHO's authority rests on systematic use of evidence.

sections.extract: The Twelfth General Programme of Work (GPW) of WHO (2014) specifies that in its normative and standard-setting work, WHO is and will remain a science- and evidence-based organization with a focus on public health. Guidelines are the fundamental means through which the Organization fulfils its technical leadership in health, as identified in the GPW. sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Lists the principles WHO guidelines must follow, after noting that WHO uses internationally recognized methods and standards. The principles include addressing a real area of uncertainty, reflecting the right to health, transparent and explicit development, multidisciplinary input, minimizing bias, systematic weighing of benefits and harms, public availability of evidence, adaptability to local settings, and tailoring to a specific audience.

sections.title: What is the aim of this handbook?

summary.text: States the aim of the handbook: to set out principles and stepwise instruction for developing a WHO guideline. Says the goal is a credible guideline whose recommendations balance benefits and harms, meet WHO publication standards, rest on accessible evidence and can be implemented to benefit population health.

sections.extract: This handbook presents the important principles of guideline development and provides stepwise instruction on the technical and procedural aspects of developing a WHO guideline. sections.title: For whom is this handbook intended?

summary.text: Lists the intended readers of the handbook: WHO staff and departments wishing to produce a guideline, members of the steering, development and external review groups, and anyone wanting to understand how WHO develops guidelines.

sections.extract: This handbook is intended for: ■■ any WHO department, programme or staff member wishing to produce a guideline; ■■ members of a WHO guideline steering group; ■■ members of a WHO guideline development group (GDG); ■■ members of a WHO guideline external review group; and ■■ anyone interested in understanding how WHO develops guidelines.

sections.title: What is in this handbook?

summary.text: Says the handbook follows guideline development from deciding whether a guideline is needed through to publication, and points to a table summarizing the process and its main contributors.

sections.extract: This handbook follows the entire development of a WHO guideline − from determining if a guideline is needed through to eventual publication. The guideline development process and its primary contributors are summarized in Table 1.1.

sections.title: Types of WHO guidelines

summary.text: Explains that the type of guideline determines methods, resources and time frame, and that types differ in purpose, scope, timing, developer, new versus existing recommendations and timeline. Names four main types (standard, consolidated, interim, and emergency or urgent-need) plus other less frequent types. Presents a table of the development process by stage, contributor, step and chapter, from planning through publishing and updating, and a table comparing each type's purpose, scope, developer, recommendations and development period.

sections.extract: It is important to consider what type of guideline will best fit the intended purpose, as this will determine the methods, resources and time frame for development, finalization and dissemination (see Table 1.2). sections.title: Standard guidelines

summary.text: Describes standard guidelines, which cover a clinical or policy area and can range from a single drug to the full scope of a condition, with recommendations either new or updated. Lists their usual focus areas such as clinical interventions, health-system policy, public health exposures, diagnostic tests and surveillance, and states they typically take 9 to 24 months, need systematic reviews and one or two group meetings, and have a review date. Notes that most WHO guidelines are of this type.

sections.extract: A standard guideline covers a clinical or policy area (e.g. the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage or the minimum requirements for the safe delivery of care to people with HIV infection). sections.title: Consolidated guidelines

summary.text: Defines a consolidated guideline as a compilation of recommendations from existing WHO guidelines or from other organizations' guidelines produced by consistent processes. Explains that it is complex to produce and maintain, that all included recommendations must be up to date and approved by the review committee, and that cross-referencing is required. Sets out when committee review is needed and the one case in which it is not.

sections.extract: A consolidated guideline (also known as a compilation of guidelines) contains recommendations from existing WHO guidelines, or from guidelines produced by other organizations that have followed processes consistent Chapter 1 Introduction 7 with those used by WHO (see Section 1.8.2). sections.title: Interim guidelines

summary.text: Describes interim guidelines, produced when guidance is requested while data are incomplete, for example for a new intervention, disease or data. Says they have a narrow scope and short shelf-life, must state when more evidence is expected, and still comply fully with the handbook's processes and standards despite pressure for speed.

sections.extract: Interim guidelines are produced when WHO is asked to provide guidance when the available data and information are most certainly incomplete, especially if additional data are anticipated in the near future. sections.title: Guidelines in response to an emergency or urgent need

summary.text: Describes guidelines produced for emergencies or urgent need and distinguishes two basic kinds. Emergency (rapid response) guidelines may rely on existing guidelines or expert opinion within hours to days but must still keep basic quality principles and document their rationale. Rapid advice guidelines follow WHO processes more closely, carry a review-by date and need committee review at both stages. Also notes that urgent recommendations outside an emergency must rest on a systematic review and meet all handbook standards.

sections.extract: Certain circumstances preclude the development of a standard guideline. This is the case when WHO must provide guidance in response to public health emergencies. Depending on the type of event or situation, such guidelines may need to be produced within hours, days, weeks or months. summary.text: Explains that WHO guidelines made for one setting may be adapted to another, for example routine obstetric care adapted for emergency settings. sections.title: The Guideline Review Committee

summary.text: Describes the Guideline Review Committee, established by the Director-General in 2007 to ensure WHO guidelines are high quality, transparently developed and evidence-based. Says it has about 30 members from all WHO regions plus external members and meets monthly.

sections.extract: The GRC was established by WHO’s Director-General in 2007 to ensure that WHO guidelines are of high quality, that they are developed using a transparent and explicit process, and that, to the extent possible, recommendations are based on evidence (3). sections.title: Terms of reference of the GRC

summary.text: Sets out the committee's terms of reference: it must approve all WHO publications containing recommendations and reviews each guideline twice, at the planning stage and after the final document is edited. Explains what each review checks, that the committee advises on process and methods but not technical content, and how its approval fits into WHO's internal clearance sequence.

sections.extract: All WHO publications containing recommendations must be approved by the GRC according to WHO policies and procedures (4). The GRC reviews every WHO guideline twice during its development – once at the initial planning stage and again after the recommendations have been developed and the guideline document has been finalized and edited. sections.extract: The GRC Secretariat has several important roles. sections.title: Who is the target audience?

summary.text: States that a guideline needs a clearly defined target audience identified early, with recommendations tailored to it. Clarifies that end-users apply the guideline while recipients receive the interventions, and warns against writing for policy-makers, managers and clinicians at once.

sections.extract: Guidelines must have a clearly defined target audience (end-user) which is identified early in the guideline development process, and the recommendations need to be tailored to that audience. sections.title: Will the recommendations in the guideline be implemented?

summary.text: States that guidelines aim to improve health and therefore must be disseminated, adopted or adapted, and implemented. Introduces the question of whether recommendations will actually be implemented.

sections.extract: implemented? The purpose of WHO guidelines is to improve the health and well-being of individuals and populations. To accomplish that, guidelines need to be disseminated, adopted or adapted, and their recommendations implemented.

sections.title: Are the guideline and its implementation within the relevant programme’s work area and budget?

summary.text: Explains that under WHO reform all work must fall within the General Programme of Work and Programme Budget, so a guideline outside that remit will be hard to justify in resources and budget.

sections.extract: programme’s work area and budget? Under the WHO reform (1) all work at WHO should fall within the scope of the General Programme of Work and Programme Budget, as agreed with WHO’s Governing Bodies. If the guideline does not fall within this remit, it will be difficult to justify the resources and budget needed to complete the work.

sections.title: Who should be involved in developing a guideline?

summary.text: Says guideline development involves many groups and people, referring to Chapter 3, and that they should be engaged from the outset.

sections.extract: Guideline development involves collaboration among a large number of groups and people (see Chapter 3). These should be engaged from the outset.

sections.title: Do you have your director’s agreement?

summary.text: States that the director's formal approval is needed before the planning proposal or final guideline goes to the review committee, and that the assistant director-general must approve the final guideline afterwards.

sections.extract: You will need your director’s formal approval before your planning proposal or your final guideline can be considered by the GRC. In addition, your ADG will need to approve the final guideline after its review and approval by the GRC.

sections.title: Have you identified experts in guideline methods?

summary.text: Says WHO staff usually commission experts in systematic reviews and guideline development to help with key questions, evidence work and turning evidence into recommendations, and that they should be identified early.

sections.extract: Generally WHO staff commission systematic review and guideline development experts to assist in formulating the key questions; identifying, assessing and synthesizing the evidence; and translating the evidence into recommendations. Such experts should be identified early in the guideline development process.

sections.extract: To produce a high-quality guideline, you will need resources to identify or perform systematic reviews, convene meetings and cover production costs. Note that WHO cannot develop guidelines using money from commercial entities (see Chapter 6). Guideline development also involves long hours of dedication by WHO staff.

sections.title: What publication types and formats are you considering?

summary.text: Advises considering the level of detail and format that users want, and budgeting for derivative products such as summaries, algorithms or wall charts, since users rarely want detail on methods. Suggests electronic versions with short paper publications may be cheaper and more practical.

sections.extract: What level of detail and format will your target audience find most useful? summary.text: Defines scoping as deciding what a guideline will and will not include, and lists what must be determined: areas of practice or policy, interventions or exposures, affected populations and important benefit and harm outcomes. Explains that scoping sets the focus and key questions and keeps the guideline manageable, and calls it one of the hardest and most important steps because a wrong scope wastes resources and leaves users uncertain.

sections.title: Types of questions

summary.text: Introduces the two basic types of questions, background and foreground, stating that background questions give context and rationale while foreground questions directly inform recommendations.

sections.extract: There are two basic types of questions: background and foreground questions. Background questions provide context and rationale for the guideline; foreground questions directly inform and underpin recommendations.

sections.title: What are GRADE evidence profiles?

summary.text: Explains that GRADE evidence profiles hold the quality assessment and a summary of findings for each important or critical outcome and key question. It says the GDG uses them as the basis for discussion, with outcomes in rows, brief judgements on quality factors and explanatory footnotes.

summary.text: States that evidence assessment is a specialized task for a methodological expert experienced with GRADE, and that commissioned review teams must have this expertise. The extraction also includes Table 9.1, a GRADE evidence profile example on cryotherapy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, with its footnotes and very low quality ratings.

summary.text: Describes the role of WHO staff in quality assessment: they must understand GRADE well enough to supervise commissioned work and advise the GDG, and in-house reviewers need in-depth knowledge. It also says GDG members should be briefed on evidence assessment before meetings, using online modules, publications or an introduction by the methodologist or GRC Secretariat.

sections.title: How is the quality of the body of evidence assessed for intervention studies?

summary.text: Explains that GRADE rates the quality of a body of evidence for each outcome as high, moderate, low or very low, not individual studies. It states that for intervention questions the starting point is study design, randomized trials versus nonrandomized and observational studies, and advises presenting different designs separately rather than pooling them in a meta-analysis.

sections.title: Five factors can lower the quality of the body of evidence for each outcome

summary.text: Explains that randomized trial evidence starts as high quality and observational evidence as low, and that five factors can lower the rating: study limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. It includes Table 9.2 defining the four quality levels, advises recording reasons for downgrading in footnotes without rating mechanically, and details the criteria for each factor, such as randomization and blinding for trials and confounding control for observational studies. It also covers how imprecision is judged by sample size and how publication bias is suspected and handled.

For both types of studies, these initial ratings can be adjusted in light of five factors: limitations in study design and execution; indirectness; imprecision; inconsistency; and publication bias (see Fig. 9.1). sections.title: Three factors can increase the quality of the evidence from observational studies

summary.text: Explains that observational evidence, low quality from the start, can be upgraded only if there is no reason to downgrade it, using three criteria: a dose-response gradient, a direction of plausible bias that would understate the effect, and a large magnitude of effect. It describes how precision and features such as rapid or consistent effects bear on upgrading, and says upgrades can be by one or two levels.

sections.extract: observational studies Observational studies are considered low quality evidence from the outset by virtue of their design. sections.title: How is the overall quality of the evidence determined?

summary.text: Explains how the GDG determines overall quality of evidence across all critical outcomes for a recommendation. The lowest quality among the critical outcomes sets the overall quality, with two exceptions where an outcome proves not to be critical or where higher-quality evidence on other critical outcomes already supports the recommendation.

sections.extract: Guideline developers review all the information from the systematic review and, if needed, reassess and make a final decision about which outcomes are critical and which ones are important in light of the recommendations that they aim to formulate. sections.title: Is GRADE applicable in all situations?

summary.text: Considers whether GRADE applies in all situations, concluding that its structured, transparent framework has been used widely and that cases where it cannot be applied are rare and need a rationale approved by the GRC. It says GRADE also covers diagnostic tests, prognosis and baseline risk, while methods for environmental exposures, economic efficiency, network meta-analyses and modelling are still under development.

sections.extract: Confusion and concerns exist as to whether GRADE is applicable to all situations in which a GDG issues a recommendation regarding an intervention. It begins a list of four further considerations that GDGs may discuss separately, starting with the priority of the problem.

sections.title: Quality of the evidence

summary.text: States, as the first row of Table 10.1, that the quality of the evidence across critical outcomes informs recommendation strength, with higher quality making a strong recommendation more likely.

sections.extract: The quality of the evidence across outcomes critical to decision-making will inform the strength of the recommendation. The higher the quality of the evidence, the greater the likelihood of a strong recommendation.

sections.title: Values and preferences

summary.text: Gives the remaining rows of Table 10.1, describing how each factor affects the likelihood of a strong recommendation: values and preferences, balance of benefits and harms, resource implications, priority of the problem, equity and human rights, acceptability and feasibility. The text under the heading is the table body, which says that greater certainty, net benefit or advantage on each factor makes a strong recommendation more likely.

sections.extract: This describes the relative importance assigned to health outcomes by those affected by them; how such importance varies within and across populations; and whether this importance or variability is surrounded by uncertainty. The less uncertainty or variability there is about the values and preferences of people experiencing the critical or important outcomes, the greater the likelihood of a strong recommendation.

sections.title: Detailed criteria that should be considered when moving from evidence to recommendations

summary.text: Gives detailed guidance on the first two criteria for moving from evidence to recommendations. It explains that higher quality evidence favours a strong recommendation, and that values and preferences concern how people rate outcomes, can be gathered through reviews, primary surveys or GDG experience, and call for a conditional recommendation when uncertain or variable.

sections.extract: moving from evidence to recommendations 10.2.1 Quality of the evidence The quality of the evidence – the degree of confidence in the estimates of effect – is a key factor in determining the strength of a recommendation (see Chapter 9). sections.title: Balance of benefits and harms

summary.text: Explains that the GDG weighs the size of benefits and harms and the relative importance of outcomes, issuing a strong recommendation when benefits clearly outweigh harms and a conditional one when the balance is uncertain or the net benefit is small.

sections.extract: When considering the balance between an intervention’s or exposure’s benefits and harms, the GDG should examine the magnitude of the effects and the relative importance of the outcomes, including any disadvantages or inconveniences associated with the intervention (as informed by data on values and preferences). If the benefits clearly outweigh the harms, a strong recommendation is likely to be issued. On the other

sections.title: Resource implications

summary.text: Explains that resource implications are normally included in recommendations and may be informed by formal economic evaluation, modelling or qualitative description. It says clearer advantages or disadvantages favour a strong recommendation, while uncertain costs favour a conditional one.

sections.extract: Resource considerations are generally included in the formulation of recommendations, unless there is a deliberate and explicit decision to omit them. In considering resource implications, the GDG can be informed by a formal economic evaluation based on estimates collected during evidence retrieval and by modelling of cost–benefit and cost–effectiveness. If a full evaluation is not possible, resource implications

sections.title: Priority of the problem

summary.text: States that GDGs should be given evidence on burden of disease, baseline risk, prevalence or incidence, which matters especially when prioritizing across interventions.

sections.extract: GDGs should consider − and be provided with − evidence about the burden of disease and the baseline risk, prevalence or incidence of the problem that is addressed. These considerations are particularly important when the GDG needs to prioritize across interventions.

sections.title: Equity and human rights

summary.text: Explains that GDGs must consider how an intervention affects equity and human rights, giving higher priority to those that increase equity, and that greater likelihood of reducing inequities and wider accessibility make a strong recommendation more likely.

sections.extract: Interventions have implications for the progressive realization of the right to health and the options given in a guideline can reduce or increase health inequities. Policies or programmes that increase equity or reduce inequity are generally assigned higher priority by GDGs than those that do not. sections.title: Acceptability

summary.text: Explains that lower acceptability of an intervention to key stakeholders makes a recommendation less likely or calls for an implementation strategy to address concerns. It lists what shapes acceptability, including who benefits, is harmed or pays, timing of effects and ethical or legal issues.

sections.extract: The lower the acceptability of an intervention to the most important stakeholders, the lower the likelihood that it will be recommended. Or, if it is recommended, the more likely it is that a strategy to address concerns about acceptability during implementation will be included in the guideline with the recommendations. Acceptability is affected by several factors, such as who benefits from an intervention and who

sections.title: Feasibility

summary.text: Explains that less feasible options, with greater implementation barriers, are less likely to be strongly recommended, and that feasibility depends on resources, programme factors, infrastructure and training.

sections.extract: The less feasible an option is (i.e. the greater the barriers to its implementation), the lesser the likelihood that the intervention will be strongly recommended. Feasibility is influenced by the resources available, programmatic considerations, the existing and the necessary infrastructure and training, and many other factors.

sections.title: Evidence-to-recommendation tables

summary.text: Describes evidence-to-recommendation tables, which show how each factor informs a recommendation, improve transparency, focus discussion and record judgements. It says the GDG should at least document the four main factors and that the review team and methodologist can prepare much of the table beforehand.

sections.extract: Evidence-to-recommendation tables depict how the factors that determine the direction and strength of a recommendation inform the process of developing the recommendation. These tables enhance the transparency of the process, focus the discussions of the GDG and permit recording of the judgements made about each factor and how each one contributed to the recommendation. sections.title: The strength of the recommendation

summary.text: Explains that recommendation strength reflects the GDG's confidence in the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences, with a strong recommendation issued when confident and a conditional (weak) one when uncertain. It refers to Table 10.2 as an interpretive aid.

sections.extract: The strength of a recommendation expresses the degree to which the GDG is confident in the balance between the desirable and undesirable consequences of implementing the recommendation. When a GDG is very certain about this balance (i.e. the desirable consequences clearly outweigh the undesirable consequences), it issues a strong recommendation in favour of an intervention. sections.title: Strong recommendations

summary.text: Explains that strong recommendations convey confidence that desirable effects outweigh undesirable ones, are uncommon because the balance is rarely certain, and call for caution when evidence quality is low or very low.

sections.extract: Strong recommendations communicate the message that the guideline is based on the confidence that the desirable effects of adherence to the recommendation outweigh the undesirable consequences. Strong recommendations are uncommon because the balance between the benefits and harms of implementing a recommendation is rarely certain. In particular, GDGs need to be cautious when considering making strong recommendations

sections.title: Conditional or weak recommendations

summary.text: Explains that conditional (weak) recommendations are made when the guideline group is less certain about the balance of benefits and harms, and that they usually state the conditions for implementing them. Includes a table interpreting strong versus conditional recommendations for patients, clinicians and policy-makers.

sections.extract: Recommendations that are conditional or weak are made when a GDG is less certain about the balance between the benefits and harms or disadvantages of implementing a recommendation. Conditional recommendations generally include a description of the conditions under which the end-user should or should not implement the recommendation. Table 10.2. sections.title: Formulating recommendations

summary.text: Describes how evidence-to-recommendation tables record the evidence, judgements and justification for a recommendation's direction and strength, along with subgroups, the formulation process, implementation issues and research gaps.

sections.extract: The evidence-to-recommendation tables depict not only the evidence and judgements leading to a recommendation, but also the justifications for the recommendation’s direction and strength. They also describe the subgroups considered, the process used to formulate recommendations (e.g. if voting took place) and key issues surrounding implementation, evaluation and monitoring (see Chapter 13) as well as research gaps.

sections.title: Reaching agreement on recommendations

summary.text: Describes how draft recommendations are prepared by the steering group or the guideline group and reviewed against GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-decision tables at the meeting. States that the group must agree on direction and strength by consensus, and that strong disagreement points to a conditional recommendation.

sections.extract: Draft recommendations can be prepared either by the steering group before the GDG meets to formulate recommendations, or during the meeting by the GDG itself. Under the leadership of the chair, the GDG reviews and discusses the GRADE evidence profiles presented by a representative of the systematic review team. sections.title: Writing recommendations

summary.text: Sets out how recommendations should be written: clear, actionable, in PICO format, in the active voice, with consistent wording and an indication of strength and evidence quality. Advises on terms such as should and suggest, prefers explicit wording like recommending against over the ambiguous not recommended, and says each recommendation needs a justification, remarks on context and links to its supporting evidence.

sections.extract: Recommendations need to be clear and actionable, reflect the PICO format and contain an indication of their strength and of the quality of the evidence on which they are based. Outcomes should generally not be mentioned in the recommendation to avoid the impression that only single outcomes are relevant or were considered. sections.title: When not to make recommendations

summary.text: Explains that a guideline group may occasionally decide the evidence is insufficient to make a recommendation, and gives a model statement for such cases. Stresses that this should be exceptional, that the lack of evidence must be stated openly, and that case reports or national experience can instead support a documented conditional recommendation.

sections.extract: In rare situations, a GDG may decide that the evidence is not sufficient to be able to formulate a recommendation. For instance, it may not be appropriate to make a recommendation when no evidence about the effects of an intervention is found, in which case the following statement could be included: “No recommendation can be made because evidence on the effectiveness (or harms) of intervention X was not identified.”

sections.title: Future research

summary.text: Explains that significant evidence gaps should be described in the guideline with suggested questions and methods for future research, possibly prioritized and framed using PICO.

sections.title: What is a rapid advice guideline?

summary.text: Introduces the rapid advice guideline as an evidence-informed guideline produced within one to three months in response to a public health emergency, following the usual steps with modifications for the accelerated timeline.

sections.extract: In response to a public health emergency, WHO must provide global leadership and timely guidance in the form of an evidence-informed guideline produced within one to three months. The steering group for such a rapid advice guideline must follow all of the basic steps for guideline development as described in this handbook, but with modifications to meet the accelerated timeline.

sections.title: What is a rapid review?

summary.text: Defines a rapid review as an evidence review using accelerated or modified systematic review methods, explaining that a standard systematic review can take six months to over a year and may be infeasible in an emergency. States that rapid reviews keep core values such as transparency and bias minimization, and lists efficiencies such as narrower scope, fewer outcomes, more reviewers in parallel and streamlined processes.

sections.extract: Because recommendations issued by WHO need to be based on the best available evidence, guidelines typically draw on evidence from well conducted and reported systematic reviews, whether they exist already or are undertaken to inform the development of the guideline. summary.text: States that little guidance and few data exist on how rapid reviews perform against standard systematic reviews, and that approaches and reporting vary widely across organizations.

summary.text: Says the first question is whether a rapid advice guideline is appropriate in the emergency, as opposed to a standard guideline or deferring development, and that this should be considered at the planning stage.

sections.extract: The first and most important question to consider is whether a rapid advice guideline is appropriate in the setting of the public health emergency at hand. summary.text: Explains how to examine the type of emergency driving the request, classing emergencies as natural, technological or conflict-related and sudden or gradual. Refers to WHO's rapid risk assessment manual and the Emergency Response Framework, including the grading of emergencies from Grade 1 to Grade 3.

Emergencies may be classified as natural, technological, or conflict-related and may be of sudden onset (e.g. earthquakes, tsunamis, chemical crises) or more gradual onset (e.g. deteriorating situations in armed conflict, progressive disease outbreaks, drought or food insecurities). summary.text: Explains that a rapid advice guideline is mainly considered for a new situation or a known event in a new context, and that for non-novel events suitable high-quality guidelines may already exist.

sections.extract: WHO staff may consider producing a rapid advice guideline primarily in the face of one of two types of events: ■■ a new situation (e.g. a new strain of influenza; the Middle East respiratory syndrome [MERS] coronavirus; or an earthquake); or ■■ an event encountered previously but causing problems in a different context (e.g. a natural disaster; a change in disease pattern such as the Ebola virus disease in West

sections.title: Does uncertainty need to be urgently addressed?

summary.text: Notes that rapid advice guidelines, like others, address uncertainty about what to do, and that the question is how quickly it must be resolved.

sections.extract: Guidelines are indicated when there is uncertainty about what to do in a specific situation. Rapid advice guidelines are no different. WHO staff may be uncertain about what advice to provide, or there may be uncertainty in the field, with different players having different viewpoints and approaches. The question here is how quickly the uncertainty needs to be addressed.

sections.title: What is the anticipated time frame for the event?

summary.text: States that rapid advice guidelines aim to give recommendations implementable within one to three months, and may be unsuitable if the event is expected to last beyond six months.

sections.extract: The intent of rapid advice guidelines is to provide urgently needed, evidence- informed recommendations that can be implemented within one to three months of the appearance of an unfolding situation or crisis. If from the outset an event is judged likely to persist beyond six months, a rapid advice guideline may not be suitable. summary.text: Says a rapid advice guideline should be developed only if dissemination and implementation mechanisms exist and are feasible, considering health systems, acceptability, training and resources. Summarizes the conditions for going ahead: a clear need, manageable scope, adequate expertise and funding, and an implementation plan.

sections.extract: Rapid advice guidelines should only be developed if a mechanism is in place for disseminating and implementing them, and if implementing the recommendations is feasible in the context of the emergency. summary.text: Introduces the development of rapid advice guidelines as following the same basic steps as standard guidelines, with differences summarized in a table.

sections.extract: The basic steps for developing a rapid advice guideline are identical to those that apply to standard guidelines, as outlined in Chapter 1. sections.title: Consult the GRC Secretariat early

summary.text: Advises the responsible technical officer to contact the Guideline Review Committee Secretariat early for guidance, help with the planning proposal and review team, and notes the committee must approve development at the planning stage for accelerated review.

sections.extract: It is particularly important for the responsible technical officer of a rapid advice guideline to contact the GRC Secretariat early in the guideline development process. summary.text: Explains that a rapid advice guideline still needs a planning proposal submitted to the review committee, in the same format as for standard guidelines. Says it should be detailed, kept up to date as a living document with rationale for changes, because the rapid review process is more fluid and documentation supports transparency.

sections.title: How do rapid reviews compare with systematic reviews?

summary.text: Contrasts rapid with standard systematic reviews: restricted search criteria, existing systematic reviews as first evidence, targeted iterative screening, less emphasis on meta-analysis and shorter reports, while keeping transparency and explicit methods.

sections.extract: reviews? The core principles of evidence searching and retrieval, including transparency and reproducible and explicit methods, apply to rapid reviews. There are key differences, however, between searching in the context of a rapid review and of a standard systematic review. sections.title: Types of rapid reviews

summary.text: Describes four types of rapid review, from a full systematic review done quickly to reviews of only systematic reviews and guidelines, or of primary studies, and refers to a figure outlining their features.

sections.extract: The reviews that underpin rapid advice guidelines may be categorized into four basic types: a full, standard systematic review performed rapidly; a review involving a variety of abbreviated methods and including only systematic reviews and existing guidelines; a review of primary studies and existing systematic reviews, or a review of primary studies only. Select the types of evidence to be collected and identify the appropriate sources

summary.text: Explains which evidence to target and where to look, emphasizing existing high-quality systematic reviews and guidelines, then primary studies, landmark papers and good observational studies as needed. Notes that rapid reviews usually search only two to three key databases.

sections.extract: the appropriate sources Depending on the nature of the question being asked, the purpose of the rapid review and the magnitude of the literature on the topic, various types of evidence may be targeted. sections.title: Develop search strategies

summary.text: Explains how to build rapid review search strategies, using subject headings and text words, with review by a team member, content experts and an information specialist. Notes that study-design filters can surface top evidence first and that a rapid review may favour precision over recall, with the choice reported.

sections.title: Search for grey literature

summary.text: Advises that a limited grey literature search, such as checking relevant organizations' websites, may be considered, in consultation with a WHO library information specialist.

sections.extract: A search for grey literature should be considered but needs to be limited. For example, the websites of relevant organizations can quickly provide relevant data. An information specialist at WHO’s headquarters library should be consulted regarding the proposed strategy for searching the grey literature.

sections.title: Common search restrictions

summary.text: Discusses common eligibility restrictions for rapid review searches, especially language limits chosen by topic, illustrated by an Ebola protective equipment review limited to English and French. Says restrictions must be documented in the proposal, report and guideline, and that titles in excluded languages should be listed in an appendix.

summary.text: Describes other ways to find evidence, such as real-time data collection like the survey of repatriated health workers during the 2014 Ebola outbreak, and scanning reference lists. Includes a box of common search restrictions covering sources, language, accessible studies, grey literature, dates and region.

sections.title: Screening and study selection

summary.text: Describes screening and study selection for rapid reviews as following standard methods, with two people independently screening titles and abstracts and two reviewers assessing full texts, reaching consensus with a third reviewer if needed. Notes that one reviewer plus a check of exclusions is an acceptable alternative at the first step.

sections.title: Data extraction and evidence synthesis

summary.text: Describes data extraction for rapid reviews: extract only information the guideline group needs, use a pilot-tested form, and have a second reviewer verify, or check a random sample of at least 10 percent.

sections.extract: Before starting data extraction, it is important to carefully consider what specific information the GDG will need to make its decisions so that only essential information is extracted. summary.text: Explains that risk of bias should be assessed for individual studies and may help select studies for inclusion. summary.text: Explains that the quality of evidence for each outcome should be assessed with GRADE, focusing on critical outcomes, and that narrative syntheses can also be graded. sections.title: Conclusions

summary.text: Concludes that rapid advice guidelines are developed in one to three months with a very narrow scope, early engagement of experts and the review committee Secretariat, and more fluid evidence review methods. Stresses that core principles of minimizing bias, transparency and meeting audience needs still apply, and that limitations and a commitment to update must be stated.

sections.extract: This chapter outlines the processes and methods used to develop a rapid advice guideline within one to three months in the context of a public health emergency. The development of a rapid advance guideline differs in important ways from the development of a standard guideline. summary.text: Describes the required guideline format: an executive summary with key recommendations, strength and evidence quality, a main body with introduction, methods, recommendations, conclusions and participant and interest details, and appendices for supporting documentation. sections.extract: All guidelines should have an executive summary, a main body and appendices. The executive summary should contain the key recommendations of the guideline. As executive summaries are often read as stand-alone documents, the strength of the recommendation and the quality of the evidence for each recommendation should be specified in the executive summary, as well as in the main body of the guideline. summary.text: Advises identifying a writer early, whether staff or freelance, estimating time and fees, with guidance on rates and a week for 5000 words. Recommends avoiding multiple authors, since unpaid chapter drafts tend to create more work.

sections.title: Legal advice on proprietary products

summary.text: Advises that guidelines should avoid naming proprietary products, describing devices and diagnostics generically and consulting WHO legal counsel if in doubt.

sections.extract: WHO guidelines should avoid specifying proprietary products when at all possible. Devices and diagnostics used in interventions should be described generically to avoid identification of specific products and trademarks. If in doubt, please contact WHO’s legal counsel.

sections.title: Editing and proofreading

summary.text: Advises engaging an editor and proofreader from lists kept by the publishing office, and booking them early because the best are reserved months ahead.

sections.extract: You will also need an editor and a proofreader. WHO press maintains lists of approved freelance technical editors, copy-editors and proofreaders and provides sample terms of reference and standard rates of pay for these tasks on the intranet. The best editors and proofreaders are often booked up many months in advance, so plan production schedules as early as possible and reserve their time accordingly.

summary.text: Explains that guidelines should carry a review-by date showing how long recommendations are expected to stay valid, set by considering the pace of research, questions without evidence and the potential need for new advice.

sections.extract: WHO guidelines should be issued with a “review-by” date to indicate how long the recommendations are expected to remain valid. There is no absolute rule about the length of validity (5, 6). In deciding on the date by which a guideline should be reviewed, take account of the rate of change of research on the topic, questions for which no evidence has been found, and the potential need for new advice.
